q: A function reaches its last line and has no `return`. What does the call give back?
why: A recipe card with no "serve" step hands over nothing. The call gives back `undefined`.

options: A `ReferenceError`: the `const` slot is locked until its line runs
why: Only the slots are made early. A `const` slot is locked until its line runs. Only a function declaration holds the whole function from the start.

q: Which of these give an error if you call them BEFORE their line?
why: A declaration is ready anywhere in the file. A `const` or `let` slot is locked, so you get a `ReferenceError`. A `var` slot holds `undefined`, so you get a `TypeError`.

q: `var c = function () {};` is on line 5, and you call `c()` on line 1. What error do you get?
why: A `var` slot is made early and holds `undefined`. Calling `undefined` is a `TypeError`. A `ReferenceError` is for a locked `let` or `const` slot.
`sayHi()` has brackets, so it runs first and gives back the text `"Hi"`. Then `run` tries to call a text. Fix: `run(sayHi)`, with no brackets.

q: What does this print? Type the two answers with a space between them.
why: With curly braces an arrow is like any function, so it needs a `return`. There is none, so the call gives `undefined`. A function is a value, and its type is `"function"`.

q: `const make = () => { id: 1 };` gives back the object `{ id: 1 }`.
why: No. JavaScript reads the curly braces as the function body, not as an object. So it gives `undefined`. To give back an object, wrap it in brackets: `() => ({ id: 1 })`.

q: Put the steps of `twice(double, 3)` in the right order. `twice` is `(fn, x) => fn(fn(x))`.
items: `twice` starts with a new box: `fn` is `double`, `x` is `3`
The inner `fn(x)` calls `double(3)` in a new box and gives `6`
The outer `fn(6)` calls `double` again in another new box and gives `12`
`twice` gives back `12`, and its box is thrown away
why: Each call gets its own new box. That is why `n = 3` and `n = 6` never mix.

q: In React, `<button onClick={handleClick()}>` causes trouble. Why?
options: The brackets call `handleClick` during render, and React gets its result, not the function
React cannot use functions as props
Nothing is wrong. Both forms work the same
why: Brackets mean "call it now". Pass `handleClick`, not `handleClick()`, so React can call it later when the click happens.

q: Which of these are true about a function in JavaScript?
options: You can store it in a variable
You can pass it into another function
You can give it back from a function with `return`
Passing it makes a second copy of the function
why: A function is a value (the interview word is first-class functions). Passing it does not copy it. Both names point at the same function.

q: Two calls of the same function share their parameters, so `n` from the first call is still there in the second.
why: No. Every call makes a new scope box, and the parameters live inside it. When the call ends, the box is thrown away.

q: What does this print? Type the three answers with spaces between them.
why: A default fills in only when no value comes in, meaning the value is `undefined`. `tag(undefined)` and `tag()` both use `"Hello"`. `null` is a real value, so `tag(null)` gives back `null`.
